questiontext.text: What is the main purpose of an inventory in server configuration management?

generalfeedback.text: An inventory identifies target hosts and groups and can associate relevant information with them. It supports selecting the appropriate targets for configuration; it is not a complete backup of their state.

answer.text: To store a complete binary snapshot of every server
To replace all reusable configuration definitions
To identify managed hosts and groups and associate relevant targeting information
To record only the operations that previously failed

questiontext.text: An automation system manages only the resources explicitly declared to it. Its declaration requires a web service but says nothing about an unrelated package installed manually. What should you expect after a successful run?

generalfeedback.text: The system in the question manages explicitly declared resources. A resource outside that scope is not automatically declared absent, so unmanaged state can remain even after successful configuration.

answer.text: The unrelated package can remain because it is outside the declared scope.
Every package not named in the declaration is automatically removed.
The machine is necessarily recreated from a stock image.
Success proves that every aspect of the machine matches a complete baseline.

questiontext.text: What is the strongest reason to organize server configuration into reusable units for common setup, web services, and databases?

generalfeedback.text: Grouping related responsibilities creates units that can be understood, reused, and maintained. Such units can still have dependencies and need integration testing; splitting files does not guarantee independence or parallelism.

answer.text: It guarantees that all configuration actions can run simultaneously.
It makes each unit independent of every other resource and input.
It removes the need to test how the units work together.
It groups related responsibilities so they can be understood, reused, and maintained separately.

name.text: L3 Q4 Configuration values and shared logic

questiontext.text: Development and production use the same service configuration logic but need different capacity values. Which organization best supports reuse and makes the intended differences clear?

generalfeedback.text: Shared logic plus explicit environment values preserves reuse and makes intentional differences reviewable. A documented configuration scheme makes the effective values understandable; copying whole definitions or hiding overrides makes divergence harder to control.

answer.text: Copy the full logic for each environment and edit the copies independently.
Keep shared logic reusable and supply explicit environment-specific values through a documented configuration scheme.
Hide the production values inside unrelated shared configuration files.
Require both environments to have identical capacity so no values differ.

questiontext.text: Web, database, and batch-processing servers all need a common baseline but different workload configuration. Which organization expresses both requirements with the least duplicated baseline logic?

generalfeedback.text: Grouping selects the appropriate targets; reusable units define the configuration to apply. Composing a common baseline with workload-specific units avoids both duplicated baseline logic and installation of every workload on every host. No particular inventory syntax or folder layout is required.

answer.text: Maintain a complete baseline copy for every workload group so each team can change it independently.
Apply every configuration unit to every server and let operators disable the unwanted services afterward.
Apply one reusable baseline to the fleet and select workload-specific units through the corresponding host groups.
Use workload groups only for connection settings and put all server configuration into one sequence applied to every host.

name.text: L3 Q6 Desired state and operational actions

questiontext.text: A service is already running and its relevant configuration has not changed. How does declaring that it should be running differ from requesting a restart on every automation run?

generalfeedback.text: A running-state declaration describes a condition that may already hold. A restart request describes an operation. Repeated execution can therefore leave a healthy service undisturbed with the first approach and disrupt it with the second. Relevant changes can still justify a restart.

answer.text: The desired-state declaration can leave it running undisturbed; an unconditional restart requests another operation and can cause unnecessary disruption.
Both requests must stop and start it again, because automation cannot confirm a running state without restarting.
The desired-state declaration starts it only on the first deployment; the restart request is the only way to recover it after a later failure.
The restart request becomes a no-op after its first success, even if the automation explicitly requests it on every run.

name.text: L3 Q7 Responding to configuration changes

questiontext.text: Several compatible configuration changes must be applied before a service reloads them. Which approach best avoids unnecessary work while activating a coherent configuration?

generalfeedback.text: Apply and validate compatible changes before activation, then reload when relevant state changed. This avoids repeated reloads and allows the service to consume a coherent configuration. A running process does not necessarily reread changed files automatically.

answer.text: Reload after every file is copied, even when its contents are unchanged, to make each step independently visible.
Apply and validate the compatible changes, then reload once if relevant configuration actually changed.
Reload before changing the files, then skip the final reload if the configuration steps report success.
Apply all changes and avoid reloading while the service remains running, because a running process always reads updated settings.

name.text: L3 Q8 Configuration success and functional success

questiontext.text: All configuration steps report success, but users cannot use the application. Which interpretation and follow-up check are most useful?

generalfeedback.text: Configuration checks establish selected resource conditions, not necessarily end-to-end behavior. A representative request can expose failures in connectivity, dependencies, or application behavior that file, package, and process checks miss. Configuration success and functional failure can coexist.

answer.text: Successful configuration proves the application works; compare automation exit codes from two consecutive runs.
The deployment must have drifted; check only whether all expected configuration files still exist.
A running service proves the application is reachable; compare installed package names with the deployment log.
Managed resources may be configured correctly while the user workflow still fails; exercise a representative request through the application and its dependencies.

questiontext.text: A growing team is considering replacing one large configuration file with reusable units and explicit environment composition. Which proposal best balances reuse with the cost of added structure?

generalfeedback.text: Coherent units support reuse and focused review, but extra interfaces and indirection can obscure dependencies and effective values. Documented inputs, visible composition, clear override rules, and integration checks address those costs. A small system may still be adequately served by a single file.

answer.text: Use coherent baseline and workload units with documented inputs and override rules; test their composition because extra interfaces can hide dependencies or conflicts.
Split every operation into its own unit and select them implicitly; the resulting file count makes ownership and effective configuration self-explanatory.
Copy each environment into its own repository; independent changes remove the need to coordinate common behavior across environments.
Keep one universal unit and add environment conditions throughout it; using one file removes the need to document how environment values interact.

name.text: L3 Q10 Checking the intended state

questiontext.text: A deployment skips software setup whenever an 'application' directory exists. The directory remains after the desired version changes, so the process reports success without inspecting the version or behavior. Which correction best establishes the intended state?

generalfeedback.text: Directory existence is not evidence of the desired software version or a complete installation. Repeated no-ops can preserve an incorrect state. Compare meaningful observed state with intended state, update when needed, and verify the result; changing a timestamp or log does not establish actual configuration.

answer.text: Keep the directory check and run the process twice; two unchanged runs establish that the desired version is installed.
Recreate the directory on every run and treat its new timestamp as proof that the application has been updated.
Compare the installed version or artifact with the desired one, repair missing or mismatched state, then verify the version and representative application behavior.
Update the deployment log with the desired version whenever the directory exists, then use that log as the check on future runs.
